title: Denver, Voting Rights Groups Sue to Block Armed ICE Agents From Polling Places
detail: The City of Denver joined the League of United Latin American Citizens, Common Cause, and UnidosUS in a federal lawsuit filed Thursday, September 10, 2026 in Washington, D.C., seeking to block the Trump administration from stationing armed ICE agents at polling sites during the November 2026 midterms. The suit, filed against DHS, Secretary Markwayne Mullin, ICE, and Acting Director David Venturella, argues that doing so would violate a Civil War-era law barring federal officials from placing armed men to 'keep the peace at the polls,' and cites a May 2024 San Antonio incident in which armed agents detained someone in view of voters and a June 2026 episode in Syracuse in which agents interrogated a polling volunteer about her social media activity. The case was assigned to U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan. Denver Mayor Mike Johnston said 'the right to vote, and to do so without fear of intimidation, is fundamental to our democracy.' Secretary Mullin responded that 'ICE isn't there to patrol the polling places. We're there to enforce specific threats... or we're serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down.'

title: Common Cause Sues DHS, DOJ and FBI Alleging Nationwide Intimidation of ICE Enforcement Observers
detail: Common Cause filed a 94-page federal lawsuit on September 10, 2026 in Washington, D.C. accusing DHS, the Justice Department, the FBI and other federal agencies of violating the First Amendment and privacy rights of people who peacefully observe ICE enforcement operations, seeking a nationwide order barring the agencies from intimidating or retaliating against observers. The complaint, drawing on declarations from seven Common Cause members in Maryland, Minnesota and New Jersey plus prior cases from Illinois, Maine and Tennessee, alleges ICE officers directed local police to bar a member from a public parking lot outside a Maryland ICE facility after running his face through a facial-recognition database; that Maine activists were told they could end up in a domestic-terrorism database or watchlist; that a California activist who tracks ICE on Instagram received an administrative subpoena seeking his identity; and that one observer, queried by law enforcement 55 times since March 2026, had his Global Entry membership revoked a day after ICE officers photographed him and told him to stop following them. DHS said in a statement that 'ICE respects the First Amendment rights of individuals to observe and express themselves' but will act if activity 'interferes with or obstructs' operations; DOJ did not respond and the FBI declined to comment.
